steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on total completion time scheduling under scenarios, where each scenario is a subset of the jobs. Define the MinMax and MinAvg problems, place them within optimization under scenarios more generally, and cover related work on scheduling with scenarios.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Classical problem: total completion time on identical parallel machines
2. Our generalization: scenarios as subsets of jobs; MinMaxSTC and MinAvgSTC
3. Optimization under scenarios
4. Scenario versions are harder than single-scenario problems
5. Related work on scheduling under scenarios

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Classical problem
- set J of n jobs, processing times p_{j}, j\in J
- one of oldest results in scheduling theory: non-decreasing processing times, identical parallel machines, round robin -> minimizes total completion time (sum of completion times)

2. Our generalization
- input also: K scenarios \mathcal{S}=\{S_{1},\dots,S_{K}\}, S_{k}\subseteq J, k=1,\dots,K
- find one parallel machine schedule for all of J: assignment of jobs to machines + order on each machine
- induces a schedule per scenario by skipping jobs not in the scenario; such jobs add nothing to that scenario's total completion time and do not delay later jobs on the same machine
- objective: function of total completion times over all scenarios
- MinMax: minimize maximum total completion time over scenarios -> MinMaxSTC (MinMax Scenario scheduling with Total Completion time objective)
- MinAvg: minimize average -> MinAvgSTC

3. Optimization under scenarios
- model uncertainty in input or different situations; many approaches under different names
- Stochastic Programming: discrete distributions over parameter values
- Sampling Average Approximation: samples, for continuous distributions
- Robust Optimization: situations to take into account, often ranges for parameter values
- data-driven optimization: scenarios as observations
- fits A Priori Optimization: schedule for all jobs = a priori solution, updated simply per scenario
- scheduling literature: overview by Shabtay and Gilenson
- Min–Max Regret: minimize max deviation over scenarios between solution value and optimal value of scenario

4. Harder than single scenario
- shortest path, scenario = destination
- metric minimum spanning tree, scenario = subset of vertices in tree
- NP-hard problems too: set cover, traveling salesperson problem

5. Related work
- focus on scheduling work close to our model; survey for overview
- Feuerstein et al.: scenarios = subsets of jobs, makespan on identical parallel machines, MinMax and MinAvg; approximation algorithms + non-approximability; our hardness results (Proposition 1) follow from their work
- multi-scenario models: discrete set of scenarios, parameters (e.g. processing times) differ per scenario; mostly single machine; various functions incl. MinMax/MinAvg
- Yang and Yu: MinMax total completion time NP-hard on single machine with 2 scenarios; in our model 2 -scenario versions generally easy; our model != processing time 0 for absent job
- Aloulou and Della Croce: algorithmic and complexity results, several single machine problems
- Mastrolilli, Mutsanas, and Svensson: MinMax weighted total completion time, single machine; approximability and inapproximability
- Kasperski and Zieliński: single machine with precedence constraints; general framework, various objectives
- Kasperski, Kurpisz, and Zieliński: parallel machines, makespan, scenario-dependent processing times; approximability for unbounded number of machines, constant number of scenarios
- Albers and Janke; Bougeret, Jansen, Poss, and Rohwedder: budgetary model, up to \Gamma jobs fail and need additional processing time; makespan; approximate algorithms for identical and unrelated machines vs. online algorithms

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
We have a set J of n jobs with given processing times p_{j}, j\in J. One of the oldest results in scheduling theory says that if we schedule the jobs in order of non-decreasing processing times on identical parallel machines in a round robin way, this minimizes the total completion time, which is the sum of the completion times of all jobs.

We study a generalization of this classical scheduling problem in which the input also gives a set of K scenarios \mathcal{S}=\{S_{1},\dots,S_{K}\}, with S_{k}\subseteq J, k=1,\dots,K. The task is to find one parallel machine schedule for the whole set of jobs J, meaning an assignment of all jobs to machines and an order of the jobs on each machine. This gives a schedule for each scenario in a natural way, by just skipping the jobs that are not in the scenario. So jobs that are not in a particular scenario do not count towards the total completion time of that scenario, and they also do not delay the later jobs on the same machine.

We want to find a schedule for the whole set of jobs that optimizes a function of the total completion times of the jobs over all scenarios. We look at two such functions: in the MinMax version we minimize the maximum total completion time over all scenarios, and in the MinAvg version we minimize the average of the total completion times over all scenarios. In the rest of the paper we call the MinMax version MinMaxSTC (MinMax Scenario scheduling with Total Completion time objective) and the MinAvg version MinAvgSTC.

Optimization under scenarios. In optimization, scenarios are often used to model uncertainty in the input, or different situations that have to be taken into account. Many approaches have been proposed and they appear in the literature under different names. Scenarios have been used to model discrete distributions over parameter values in Stochastic Programming, and as samples in Sampling Average Approximation algorithms for stochastic problems with continuous distributions over parameter values. In Robust Optimization, scenarios describe different situations that should be taken into account, and they are often given as ranges for the parameter values that may occur. Also, in data-driven optimization, scenarios are often obtained as observations. Our problems also fit in the general framework of A Priori Optimization: the schedule for all the jobs can be seen as an a priori solution that is updated in a simple way to get a solution for each scenario. In scheduling, different ways of modeling scenarios have been introduced, and for these we refer to a very recent overview by Shabtay and Gilenson. Another related framework, which is popular, is Min–Max Regret, where the aim is a solution that minimizes the maximum deviation, over all possible scenarios, between the value of the solution and the optimal value of the corresponding scenario.

For many problems, the versions with multiple scenarios are fundamentally harder than the single scenario versions, which is not surprising. Examples are the shortest path problem where a scenario is given by the destination, and the metric minimum spanning tree problem where a scenario defines the subset of vertices that has to be in the tree. Scenario versions of NP-hard combinatorial optimization problems have also been studied, for example set cover and the traveling salesperson problem.

Related work.
- scheduling work closer to our model; survey and references therein for overview
- Feuerstein et al.: also scenarios = subsets of jobs; makespan on identical parallel machines, MinMax and MinAvg; approximation algorithms + non-approximability; hardness results in Proposition 1 follow directly from their work
- multi-scenario models: discrete set of scenarios, parameters (e.g., processing times) differ per scenario; mostly single machine; various functions with MinMax/MinAvg as special cases
- Yang and Yu: MinMax total completion time NP-hard on a single machine with only 2 scenarios; in our model 2 -scenario versions generally easy (not the same as processing time 0 for absent jobs)
- Aloulou and Della Croce: algorithmic + computational complexity results, several single machine problems
- Mastrolilli, Mutsanas, and Svensson: MinMax weighted total completion time, single machine; approximability and inapproximability results
- Kasperski and Zieliński: single machine with precedence constraints; general framework, various objectives
- Kasperski, Kurpisz, and Zieliński: parallel machines, makespan, scenario-dependent processing times; unbounded number of machines, constant number of scenarios
- Albers and Janke; Bougeret, Jansen, Poss, and Rohwedder: budgetary model, regular processing time, up to \Gamma jobs fail per scenario; makespan; approximate algorithms (identical + unrelated machines) vs. online algorithms

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
We have a set J of n jobs with given processing times p_{j}, j\in J. One of the oldest results in scheduling theory says that if we schedule the jobs in order of non-decreasing processing times on identical parallel machines in a round robin way, this minimizes the total completion time, which is the sum of the completion times of all jobs.

We study a generalization of this classical scheduling problem in which the input also gives a set of K scenarios \mathcal{S}=\{S_{1},\dots,S_{K}\}, with S_{k}\subseteq J, k=1,\dots,K. The task is to find one parallel machine schedule for the whole set of jobs J, meaning an assignment of all jobs to machines and an order of the jobs on each machine. This gives a schedule for each scenario in a natural way, by just skipping the jobs that are not in the scenario. So jobs that are not in a particular scenario do not count towards the total completion time of that scenario, and they also do not delay the later jobs on the same machine.

We want to find a schedule for the whole set of jobs that optimizes a function of the total completion times of the jobs over all scenarios. We look at two such functions: in the MinMax version we minimize the maximum total completion time over all scenarios, and in the MinAvg version we minimize the average of the total completion times over all scenarios. In the rest of the paper we call the MinMax version MinMaxSTC (MinMax Scenario scheduling with Total Completion time objective) and the MinAvg version MinAvgSTC.

Optimization under scenarios. In optimization, scenarios are often used to model uncertainty in the input, or different situations that have to be taken into account. Many approaches have been proposed and they appear in the literature under different names. Scenarios have been used to model discrete distributions over parameter values in Stochastic Programming, and as samples in Sampling Average Approximation algorithms for stochastic problems with continuous distributions over parameter values. In Robust Optimization, scenarios describe different situations that should be taken into account, and they are often given as ranges for the parameter values that may occur. Also, in data-driven optimization, scenarios are often obtained as observations. Our problems also fit in the general framework of A Priori Optimization: the schedule for all the jobs can be seen as an a priori solution that is updated in a simple way to get a solution for each scenario. In scheduling, different ways of modeling scenarios have been introduced, and for these we refer to a very recent overview by Shabtay and Gilenson. Another related framework, which is popular, is Min–Max Regret, where the aim is a solution that minimizes the maximum deviation, over all possible scenarios, between the value of the solution and the optimal value of the corresponding scenario.

For many problems, the versions with multiple scenarios are fundamentally harder than the single scenario versions, which is not surprising. Examples are the shortest path problem where a scenario is given by the destination, and the metric minimum spanning tree problem where a scenario defines the subset of vertices that has to be in the tree. Scenario versions of NP-hard combinatorial optimization problems have also been studied, for example set cover and the traveling salesperson problem.

Related work. As said above, many approaches to optimization under scenarios appear in the literature under different names. Here we mention work in scheduling that is more closely related to our model. For an overview of scheduling under scenarios we refer to the survey and the references in it.

The work closest to our problems is that of Feuerstein et al.. They also consider scenarios given by subsets of jobs, and they develop approximation algorithms and non-approximability results for minimizing the makespan on identical parallel machines, for both the MinMax and the MinAvg version. The hardness results for our problem given in Proposition 1 below actually follow directly from their work.

In multi-scenario models, there is a discrete set of scenarios, and some parameters of the jobs (e.g., processing times) can have different values in different scenarios. Several papers use this model, mostly for single machine scheduling problems. They consider various functions of the scheduling objectives over the scenarios, and the MinMax and MinAvg versions are special cases of these. For example, Yang and Yu study a multi-scenario model and show that the MinMax version of minimizing total completion time is NP-hard even on a single machine and with only 2 scenarios, while in our model 2 -scenario versions are generally easy. (Our model is not the same as just giving a job processing time 0 in a scenario when the job is not in that scenario.) Aloulou and Della Croce give algorithmic and computational complexity results for several single machine scheduling problems. Mastrolilli, Mutsanas, and Svensson look at the MinMax version of minimizing the weighted total completion time on a single machine and prove interesting approximability and inapproximability results. Kasperski and Zieliński look at a more general single machine scheduling problem with precedence constraints between jobs, and they propose a general framework for solving such problems with various objectives.

Kasperski, Kurpisz, and Zieliński study multi-scenario scheduling on parallel machines with the makespan objective, where the processing time of each job depends on the scenario. They give approximability results for an unbounded number of machines and a constant number of scenarios. Albers and Janke and also Bougeret, Jansen, Poss, and Rohwedder study a budgetary model where job processing times are uncertain. In this model each job has a regular processing time, and in each scenario up to \Gamma jobs fail and need additional processing time. The objective is to minimize the makespan. The second of these proposes approximate algorithms for identical and unrelated parallel machines, while the first one analyses online algorithms in this setting.

Aloulou and Della Croce [13] present algorithmic and computational complexity results for several single machine scheduling problems. Mastrolilli, Mutsanas, and Svensson [14] consider the MinMax version of minimizing the weighted total completion time on a single machine and prove interesting approximability and inapproximability results. Kasperski and Zieliński [15] consider a more general single machine scheduling problem with precedence constraints between jobs and propose a general framework for solving such problems with various objectives.

Kasperski, Kurpisz, and Zieliński [16] study multi-scenario scheduling with parallel machines and the makespan objective, where the processing time of each job depends on the scenario; they give approximability results for an unbounded number of machines and a constant number of scenarios. Albers and Janke [17] as well as Bougeret, Jansen, Poss, and Rohwedder [18] study a budgetary model with uncertain job processing times, in which each job has a regular processing time while in each scenario up to \Gamma jobs fail and require additional processing time. The objective is to minimize the makespan: [18] proposes approximate algorithms for identical and unrelated parallel machines, while [17] analyses online algorithms in this setting.
